strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: preference optimization/alignment for discrete diffusion models, which are increasingly relevant for language, DNA, and protein generation.
The stepwise decomposition idea is intuitive and, if correctly formalized, could enable efficient likelihood and reward evaluation compared to trajectory-level RL or backpropagation through sampling.
Extensive empirical evaluation across three domains (DNA design, protein inverse folding, language modeling) with consistent improvements over strong baselines such as DRAKES and LLaDA-8B-Instruct.
The proposed loss generalizes DPO-style pairwise preference optimization and supports arbitrary rewards with a tunable number of Monte Carlo samples N.
Ablation studies on β, N, and iterative labeling provide useful practical insights.
The paper is generally well written and clear in its high-level motivation and experimental presentation.
weaknesses: Major theoretical inconsistency: in Eq. 10 the stepwise reward is defined as \hat{r}_t(x_t,c)=E_{p(x0|xt,c)}[r(x0,c)], which is a function only of x_t. Consequently, the optimal posterior in Eq. 10 reduces to p_ref(x0|xt,c) up to a constant independent of x0, so the stepwise objective in Eq. 9 does not actually align p(x0|xt) toward high r(x0). This undermines the central claim of stepwise alignment.

The derivation of the empirical loss is inconsistent with the stated objective: Eq. 11 suggests \tilde{p}_r ∝ p_ref exp(\hat{r}_t(x_t,c)), which is constant in x0, but Eq. 12 uses weights exp(r(x0,c)), i.e., a reward that depends on x0. The appendix derivation replaces \hat{r}_t(x_t,c) with r(x0,c) without justification, so Proposition 4.2 and Theorem 4.1 do not establish the claimed equivalence for the actual algorithm.

Theorem 4.1 is therefore either trivial (for a reward constant in x0 given x_t) or incorrect for the intended stepwise objective. The claimed equivalence between stepwise decomposition and trajectory alignment is not valid as stated.

The Monte Carlo implementation in Eq. 13 samples x0 and then x_t via q(x_t|x0), which does not match the theoretical requirement of sampling x0 from p_ref(x0|x_t,c) for a fixed x_t. The self-normalized denominator mixes samples with different x_t, introducing bias that is not accounted for by Proposition 4.3.

Empirical superiority is not consistent across all metrics: on protein inverse folding, success rate and scRMSD are slightly worse than DRAKES, despite claims of outperforming baselines. Language modeling improvements are modest and only compared to the reference model, not to other alignment methods.
Reproducibility is limited: no code or model checkpoints are provided, and several training details (e.g., precise data splits, reward model checkpoints) rely on external work.
The work briefly acknowledges reward-model risk but provides no concrete mechanism to detect or mitigate harmful/noisy reward models.

strengths: Targets an important and underexplored problem: reward alignment and preference optimization for masked discrete diffusion models.

The proposed loss is a reasonable listwise extension of DPO to masked diffusion and is compatible with arbitrary reward functions; it reduces to a DPO-style pairwise objective under Bradley-Terry rewards.

Experiments cover three distinct domains and show encouraging empirical gains, especially on DNA sequence design and protein stability (predicted ddG), plus modest improvements on LLaDA-8B-Instruct benchmarks.
The paper is generally well organized and includes detailed appendices with proofs, hyperparameters, and additional results.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is incorrect/inconsistent. Eq. 9's per-step optimum should be p*(x0|xt,c) ∝ p_ref(x0|xt,c) exp(r(x0,c)/β_t), not with \hat{r}_t(xt,c). Since \hat{r}_t depends only on xt, the exponential is constant over x0 and cancels in normalization, implying p*(x0|xt,c)=p_ref(x0|xt,c). Thus the claimed stepwise alignment does not modify the posterior. The proof of Theorem 4.1 mishandles this normalization, so the equivalence to trajectory alignment is unsupported.

There is a serious mismatch between definitions and implementation. Eq. 11 defines \tilde{p}_r with \hat{r}_t(xt,c), which is constant in x0, but Eq. 12 and Appendix A.3 use exp(r(x0,c)) weights. The derivation replaces \hat{r}_t with r(x0) without justification. Proposition 4.2 therefore does not establish the optimality of the actual loss.

The empirical loss in Eq. 13 is not an unbiased estimate of Eq. 12: Eq. 12 requires x0 ~ p_ref(x0|xt,c) for fixed xt, while Eq. 13 samples x0 from the data/reference marginal and xt via q(xt|x0). The importance-sampling justification is not valid under this sampling scheme.

Evaluation and claims are not fully convincing. In the main protein table, SDPO underperforms DRAKES on scRMSD and success rate, contradicting the abstract's claim of 'consistently' superior performance; the appendix later reports a different run/checkpoint. Baselines are copied from prior work rather than re-run, and the language experiments lack comparisons to DPO or other discrete diffusion alignment baselines and report no variance.

Hyperparameter choices (very low β in later stages, staged iterative labeling, N up to 918) raise concerns about tuning and overfitting, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed decomposition rather than to reward over-optimization or extra labeling.

If the flawed theory is removed, the method reduces to a listwise DPO-style objective for masked diffusion. The paper does not sufficiently distinguish its algorithmic contribution from prior diffusion-DPO work beyond the discrete masked setting.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code release is mentioned, many evaluation details depend on prior work, and the sampling/grouping procedure for N samples per context is unclear for unconditional tasks.

strengths: Proposes a principled and novel stepwise decomposition for aligning masked discrete diffusion models, avoiding costly backpropagation through the full discrete trajectory and enabling efficient reward/likelihood evaluation on clean sequences x0.
Derives a general distribution-matching objective compatible with arbitrary reward functions, and shows it subsumes DPO/Bradley-Terry preference optimization as a special case.

Provides theoretical analysis including Theorem 4.1 (equivalence under additive factorization) and Proposition 4.3 (asymptotic unbiasedness), which, if correct, would give a solid foundation for diffusion alignment.

Extensive empirical evaluation across DNA sequence design, protein inverse folding, and language modeling, with notable gains such as ~12% DNA activity improvement over DRAKES and GSM8K improvement from 78.6 to 80.7 on LLaDA-8B-Instruct.
Includes useful ablations on sample size N, KL regularization β, and iterative labeling, along with detailed hyperparameters in the appendix.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation appears inconsistent: Eq. 10/Eq. 11 use the stepwise expected reward \hat{r}_t(x_t,c)=E[r(x0)|x_t], which is constant in x0 for fixed x_t. Consequently, the claimed optimal posterior would collapse to the reference posterior and would not maximize r(x0), while the empirical loss in Eq. 12/Eq. 13 targets exp(r(x0)). This undermines the stated equivalence unless corrected.

Theorem 4.1 relies on an additive factorization of the trajectory reward over stepwise expected rewards. This is a strong assumption that is not naturally satisfied by the original empirical reward r(x0,c), so the practical implication of the equivalence is limited.

The language-modeling evaluation lacks direct alignment baselines: it compares only against the reference LLaDA-8B-Instruct model and not against DPO-style or other preference-optimization methods adapted to discrete diffusion, making the source of improvement less clear.

On protein inverse folding, SDPO improves Pred-ddG but underperforms DRAKES on scRMSD and success rate in the main table; the appendix reports a different run with better balance, raising questions about consistency and over-optimization.

The DNA and protein experiments rely on iterative relabeling and, in some stages, very large N (e.g., 918), while many baseline numbers are taken from prior work. Fairness of comparison and computational cost are not fully discussed.
Some central claims, such as offering a 'principled' and theoretically guaranteed trajectory alignment, are stronger than the current evidence due to the above theoretical inconsistency.

strengths: Proposes a novel stepwise decomposition for offline preference optimization of discrete diffusion models, avoiding expensive online RL or full-trajectory backpropagation while enabling exact likelihood/reward evaluation on clean sequences.

Provides a theoretical connection between per-step posterior alignment and trajectory-level alignment under an additive factorization of the chain reward, yielding a principled generalized objective and recovering DPO/Bradley-Terry as a special case.
Derives a flexible loss compatible with arbitrary reward functions and Monte-Carlo estimation, with useful discussions of the roles of beta, w(t), N, and iterative labeling.

Conducts experiments across three distinct domains: DNA sequence design, protein inverse folding, and language modeling. Results show substantial gains, e.g., +12.3% Pred-Activity over DRAKES on DNA and GSM8K improvement from 78.6 to 81.2 on LLaDA-8B-Instruct.
Includes useful ablations on beta, sample size N, iterative labeling, and dataset size, with hyperparameters and implementation details largely provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The loss derivation in Appendix A.3 appears mathematically inconsistent: the conditional KL objective in Eq. 8 should use the conditional normalizer E_{p_ref(x0|xt)}[exp(r)] as the importance weight, but Eq. 9 uses a global normalizer E_{p_ref(x0)}[exp(r)]. This makes the stated equivalence between Eq. 8 and Eq. 9 questionable and the practical Monte-Carlo estimate potentially biased beyond the acknowledged Z_theta approximation.

Theorem 4.1 only guarantees that the induced joint is optimal for a specially constructed chain reward of the form beta * sum_t r_t, not for the original user reward r(x0,c) applied to the final output. Thus the claimed equivalence to trajectory alignment is narrower than the paper’s framing suggests.

On protein inverse folding, the main table shows SDPO underperforming DRAKES on success rate (75.5 vs 78.6) and scRMSD<2 (88.9 vs 91.8). The appendix reports a better SDPO run that matches success rate but lower Pred-ddG, creating concerns about selective reporting and mixed evidence for the central claim of consistent superiority.

Language-model experiments compare only against D2-DPO, omitting relevant recent discrete-diffusion alignment baselines such as VRPO or online RL methods. No variance or statistical significance is reported for the LLaDA-8B results, making the improvements harder to interpret.

Some baseline numbers are taken from prior work, and SDPO uses iterative reward labeling, giving it additional labeled data relative to some baselines. Although the paper argues greater labeling efficiency, the comparison is not fully apples-to-apples.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release or checkpoints are mentioned, and although hyperparameters are provided, exact reproduction of the large-scale LLaDA fine-tuning may be difficult.

There are minor notation and presentation issues in the appendix, including inconsistent equation numbering, missing exponential terms in some proof lines, and heavy notation that could obscure the key theoretical arguments.

strengths: Proposes a stepwise decomposition for aligning discrete diffusion models, with a general reward-based formulation that goes beyond Bradley-Terry pairwise preference.
Derives a tractable distribution-matching objective and provides theoretical analysis attempting to connect per-step posterior alignment to trajectory alignment.
Evaluates on three diverse domains (DNA design, protein inverse folding, language modeling) and reports strong improvements, especially on DNA Pred-Activity/ATAC and on LLaDA-8B GSM8K.
Provides implementation details and hyperparameters, and briefly discusses limitations and broader impact.
weaknesses: Theorem 4.1 does not establish equivalence to the original alignment objective with reward r(x0,c); it only constructs a new additive chain reward whose definition depends on the reference model and the stepwise beta_t. The induced marginal over x0 is generally not p_ref(x0) exp(r/beta), so the claimed trajectory-alignment equivalence is substantially weaker than stated.

The empirical objective in Eqs. 10-11 is not a valid Monte Carlo estimator of Eq. 9: the denominator sums exp(tilde r_theta(x0_j, x_t_j)) over samples with different x_t_j, whereas Z_theta^t must condition on the same x_t. The authors acknowledge this bias but still present the method as theoretically grounded; this undermines the central theoretical guarantees and the DPO special-case connection.

The choice beta_t = beta/w(t) with w(t)=1-alpha_t further breaks the claimed equivalence to clean-data reward alignment; the telescoping sum yields an effective reward involving w(1)r/beta and a partition term, not r(x0)/beta.

Experimental comparisons are not apples-to-apples for DNA/protein: SDPO uses iterative re-labeling (20k/12.8k extra labels) while several offline baselines do not, making the gains difficult to attribute to the alignment objective rather than extra reward labels.

Protein inverse folding results are inconsistent: Table 2 reports SDPO with worse scRMSD and success rate than DRAKES, while Appendix Table 10 reports a different SDPO run matching DRAKES success; the paper does not reconcile or clearly identify the final configuration.
Language modeling evaluation lacks variance/error bars and compares only against D2-DPO among alignment methods; improvements on AlpacaEval are small in absolute terms and could be noisy.
Reproducibility is limited by absence of code and unclear data splits/seeds for some baselines; reliance on baselines' numbers from prior work without reimplementation further weakens evaluation.
No detailed practical computational cost analysis despite N up to 918; the biased estimator may require large N, limiting scalability.

strengths: Introduces a principled stepwise decomposition for aligning discrete diffusion models, turning trajectory-level alignment into per-step posterior matching.

Provides Theorem 4.1 linking stepwise posterior alignment to trajectory alignment under an additive chain reward, and derives a general distribution-matching loss that supports arbitrary rewards rather than only Bradley-Terry preferences.
The method is offline in its standard form, avoids online sampling during finetuning, and is tailored to masked discrete diffusion while reducing to a DPO-like pairwise objective as a special case.

Comprehensive experiments across DNA sequence design, protein inverse folding, and LLM alignment with LLaDA-8B-Instruct; results are strong, including +12.3% Pred-Activity over DRAKES on DNA and GSM8K improvement from 78.6 to 81.2.
Ablations on beta, sample size N, and iterative labeling are informative, and hyperparameters, complexity, and implementation details are largely reported.
weaknesses: The theoretical equivalence is narrower than the framing suggests: Theorem 4.1 shows stepwise-optimal posteriors induce an optimum for a constructed additive chain reward, but it does not directly prove that optimizing per-step posteriors yields the sequence-level target p_ref(x0) exp(r(x0)/beta)/Z for arbitrary reward r(x0).

The practical Monte-Carlo objective in Eq. 10 estimates the partition function Z_theta^t by summing over samples with different x_t, rather than conditioning on a fixed x_t as required by the theoretical derivation; the authors acknowledge this bias, but it weakens exactness.

On protein inverse folding, the main table shows SDPO improves predicted ddG but has worse scRMSD and lower success rate than DRAKES (75.5% vs 78.6%); the stronger balanced result appears mainly in the appendix, so the main-text claim of comparable structure quality is slightly overstated.

Some baseline numbers are copied from prior work rather than re-run under a unified protocol, and the LLM evaluation is limited to a few benchmarks without variance or seed reporting, which somewhat limits reproducibility and confidence in the language-model gains.
Computational and memory costs scale with N (up to hundreds or thousands of samples per context), which may be a practical concern despite the provided complexity analysis.
